# Serving in Production: Readiness, Rollouts and Latency Regressions

Last verified: 2026-10-28 against the Kubernetes probes docs, the Open Inference Protocol (KServe) REST spec, Triton protocol and model-configuration docs, and the gRPC deadlines guide.

Scope: general model-serving operations, using public tools (Kubernetes, which runs and restarts containers across machines, and its probes, its health checks; gRPC, a binary request/response protocol; the KServe v2 protocol, a community API for model servers that the endpoints of Triton, NVIDIA's model server, are based on) as examples. This lesson says nothing about how any particular company's serving stack is built. In week 1, replace the generic nouns below with the real ones.

Builds on: Kubernetes pods and probes (lesson containers-ci/03-kubernetes-for-a-service-engineer); the request stages and queue (lessons inference-runtimes/01-serving-anatomy, 02-batching-and-scheduling).

## The problem and why it matters

A model server that works on a laptop fails in production in boring ways: traffic arrives before the model is loaded, a new model version is slower, a retry doubles the load, and nobody can tell which hop (one step in a request's path between services) added the time. Operating it means answering four questions fast: is it up, is it ready, which version is serving, and where did the time go.

## First principles

1. **Alive and ready are different.** Alive means the process is not wedged (stuck). Ready means it can serve traffic well right now. Mixing them causes restart loops or traffic to cold pods (Kubernetes' running copies of your server that have not warmed up).
2. **Ready must mean warm.** Loading weights, building or loading engines, compiling and filling caches take time. Traffic before that finishes lands on the slowest path.
3. **A model version is a deployment.** Weights, runtime, converted engine, preprocessing and config together change behaviour. Roll them out, observe them and roll them back like code.
4. **You cannot fix what you cannot split.** Queue time, batch size, per-stage latency and memory per model version are the minimum metrics. Without them every regression looks the same.
5. **Every hop needs a deadline** (a time limit after which the caller gives up). gRPC's guide says no deadline is set by default and recommends always setting a realistic one. A request with no deadline can wait forever and hold resources.
6. **Retries need idempotency and budgets.** Idempotent means repeating a request has the same effect as doing it once; a budget caps total retries. Retrying a pure prediction is usually safe. Retrying something that has side effects, or retrying everything during overload, is not.

## How it works

### Health, readiness and startup

```
 container starts
     │
     ▼
 ┌─────────────┐ startup probe passes
 │ LOADING     │ (weights, engines, warmup)
 │ not ready   │──────────────┐
 └─────────────┘              ▼
                       ┌────────────┐
   readiness fails     │ READY      │ gets traffic
   ┌───────────────────│ live+ready │
   ▼                   └─────┬──────┘
 ┌──────────────┐            │ liveness fails
 │ NOT READY    │            ▼
 │ (drained,    │      container restarted
 │  no traffic) │
 └──────────────┘
```

Kubernetes' docs: a **startup probe** gates the other probes until it succeeds, so slow-loading apps are not killed early, and if it fails the kubelet (Kubernetes' per-machine agent) kills the container. A **liveness probe** failure means restart. A **readiness probe** failure removes the pod from the matching Services' endpoints (the list of pods that receive traffic); it does not restart it. Readiness runs for the container's whole life, so a pod can leave and rejoin rotation (the set receiving traffic), for example while swapping a model.

The KServe v2 inference protocol (Triton's HTTP and gRPC endpoints are based on it, plus Triton's own extensions) defines `GET v2/health/live` (server can receive and respond to requests), `GET v2/health/ready` (all models are ready for inferencing) and `GET v2/models/<name>[/versions/<v>]/ready` (one model). The spec says the live and ready APIs can be used directly for the Kubernetes liveness and readiness probes. Triton's model-configuration docs say that when a model config defines warmup, Triton will not show the model as ready until warmup has completed. That covers only the warmup you configured, so gate your own readiness on a real warm request if your warmup misses shapes.

```yaml
startupProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /v2/health/ready, port: 8000 }   # example path and port
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 60        # allows a long load; tune to your model
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /v2/health/live, port: 8000 }
  periodSeconds: 10
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /v2/health/ready, port: 8000 }
  periodSeconds: 5
```

Probe field names are standard Kubernetes; the numbers are placeholders for illustration. Not run here (no cluster).

### Warmup and hot-swap

Warmup means running the shapes and batch sizes you expect before taking traffic, so engine build (lesson 03), `torch.compile`, allocator growth (the GPU memory pool expanding; lesson 04) and caches are paid up front. A bad warmup covers one shape; production uses ten.

```
 time ───────────────────────────────────────▶
 v1: ███████ serving ████████████ drain ┐
 v2:   load ─▶ warm ─▶ ready ██ serving │
                  ▲        │            ▼
                  │        └ flip traffic  unload v1
                  └ needs memory for both
                    (or a second replica)
```

Draining means finishing in-flight requests while accepting no new ones. Two ways to replace a model. **Replica rollout:** start new pods with v2, wait for ready, shift traffic, remove old pods. Simple and safe; costs spare capacity. **In-process hot-swap:** load v2 beside v1, warm it, flip the pointer, drain and unload v1. Saves pods but needs GPU memory for both and shares fate: a bad v2 can OOM the process serving v1. For rollback, keep v1's artifacts available and the switch cheap. Record the model version in logs, metrics labels and, where useful, a response header.

### What to export

- **Per stage latency** (decode, preprocess, queue, forward, postprocess) as histograms (counts per latency range), not averages.
- **Queue depth and queue time**, plus rejects and timeouts.
- **Batch size distribution** (mean hides the story) and padding ratio if you have it.
- **GPU utilisation and memory:** used, plus the framework's allocated and reserved.
- **Errors by type**, **model version** as a label, **cold start duration**.

### Tracing a request

```
 client ─▶ gateway ─▶ server ─▶ [queue] ─▶ [forward]
   │          │         │          │           │
   └──────────┴─────────┴──────────┴───────────┘
        one trace id, one span per box
        (id passed in headers / gRPC metadata)
```

A trace is the record of one request's whole journey, and a span is one timed step in it; the gateway is the front service that receives outside traffic. Pass one trace id through every hop so a slow request can be read as a timeline: gateway time, network, queue wait, preprocess, forward, postprocess. Inside the server, spans for queue and forward are what separate "too much load" from "slow model". Use whatever tracing standard your platform uses; the header format was not checked here.

### Integrating an engine into a pipeline

- **Protocol:** gRPC gives typed contracts (a schema both sides check), streaming and deadlines; HTTP/JSON is easy to debug but heavier for tensors. Either way, send large tensors by reference or in binary, not as JSON text, when you can.
- **Deadlines:** the client sets one; the server drops queued work already past it. gRPC's docs say that on expiry the client fails the RPC with `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED`, and that propagation (passing the remaining time on) of an incoming deadline to outgoing calls is supported by some implementations and must be enabled in some.
- **Retries:** retry only on retryable errors (overload, transient network), with exponential backoff (waiting longer after each failure), jitter (randomising the wait so clients do not retry in lockstep) and a cap on total retries. Make the request id the idempotency key so duplicates are recognisable.

### Canarying a new model

A canary is a trial release to a small slice of traffic: send a small share to v2, compare v2 against v1 on latency per stage, errors and a quality signal, and promote in steps. Shadow traffic (run v2 on copies of requests and discard its output) tests load and speed with no user risk. A canary only helps if the metrics are labelled by version and you decided the rollback criteria before starting.

## Worked failure scenario

**Symptom:** after promoting model v2 to all traffic, p99 latency is noticeably higher and some requests time out. Accuracy checks look fine.

1. **Stop the bleeding.** If v1 is still available and the rollback is cheap, roll back first; investigate with v2 in a canary or staging.
2. **Confirm it is v2.** Compare p50/p99 by the version label, and check for coincident changes: traffic mix, a new client, node pool, driver.
3. **Which stage grew?** Per-stage histograms. Queue up: capacity or batcher. Forward up: model or runtime. Preprocess up: tokenizer (the code that splits text into tokens) or image code changed with the model.
4. **If forward grew:** did the model get bigger or its outputs longer? Did the runtime change (fell back to CPU nodes, new precision, engine not rebuilt for this GPU, wrong profile range)? Compare the registered providers and engine file in a good and a bad pod.
5. **If only the first requests are slow:** warmup was incomplete. Compare cold and warm latency; add the missing shapes to warmup.
6. **If memory or batch size changed:** v2 may need a smaller max batch, causing a lower throughput and a longer queue.
7. **If errors rose with latency:** check retries. Timeouts plus retries amplify load.

**Fix:** roll back, then reproduce in staging (a production-like test environment) with recorded traffic, fix the cause (warmup list, profile range, batch limits, engine rebuild), and re-canary with the same dashboards. Add a pre-promotion gate: latency per stage within an agreed tolerance of v1, measured on warm replicas.

## Tradeoffs

| Use when | Avoid when |
|---|---|
| Replica rollout: you can afford spare GPUs, want a clean rollback | GPUs are scarce and each pod is expensive to warm |
| In-process hot-swap: fast swaps, memory for two models | Memory is tight, or a failure must not affect the live model |
| Shadow traffic: new model's speed is the risk | Outputs have side effects or the model is costly to run twice |
| Strict readiness (real warm request) | A slow health check would cause flapping |
| gRPC with deadlines: internal service calls | Public clients that need plain HTTP |

## Interview questions

1. What is the difference between liveness and readiness? *Probe:* what should a model server's readiness check? *Outline:* alive means not wedged, ready means loaded and warm; restart versus removal from endpoints; startup probe for long loads.
2. How do you roll out a new model safely? *Outline:* version label, canary or shadow, per-version metrics, preset rollback criteria, cheap rollback.
3. After deploying a new model p99 is worse. Walk me through it. *Outline:* the seven-step walk above.
4. Why does warmup matter and what goes wrong with a partial warmup? *Outline:* one-off costs (compilation, engine build, allocator growth) land on users.
5. What metrics would you put on a model server dashboard? *Outline:* per-stage latency histograms, queue time and depth, batch size, GPU use and memory, errors, version.
6. How should clients call a model server? *Probe:* retries? *Outline:* deadlines, bounded retries with backoff and jitter, idempotency keys, propagate deadlines.
7. How would you trace a request through a model server? *Outline:* trace id across hops, spans for queue and forward.

**Worked exercise:** draw the timeline of a replica rollout from "v2 pod starts" to "v1 pod removed". Mark startup, readiness, the first traffic, and the metric you would watch at each step to decide whether to continue or roll back.

## Checklist

1. I can explain liveness, readiness and startup probes and what each failure does.
2. I can describe a warmup that covers the shapes production uses.
3. I can compare replica rollout with in-process hot-swap.
4. I can list the metrics that separate queue, model and preprocessing problems.
5. I can walk a post-update latency regression to a cause and a rollback.

## Common wrong answers

- "Readiness is just port open." The model may not be loaded or warm.
- "Restart it on any failed health check." Readiness failure should drain, not restart.
- "Retry until it works." Overload plus retries is a self-inflicted outage.
- "Accuracy is fine, so ship it." Latency, memory and tail behaviour are part of correctness.

## Sources

Consulted and checked:
- Kubernetes probes (https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/probes/): startup probe holds off liveness and readiness until it succeeds and the kubelet kills the container if it fails; liveness failure restarts the container; readiness failure makes the EndpointSlice controller remove the Pod's IP from matching Services; readiness runs for the container's whole life; default `periodSeconds` is 10 s. First 100k of 118k characters read.
- Open Inference Protocol (KServe) REST spec (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kserve/open-inference-protocol/main/specification/protocol/inference_rest.md): live, ready and model-ready paths and meanings.
- Triton inference protocols (https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/triton-inference-server/user-guide/docs/customization_guide/inference_protocols.html): endpoints "based on standard inference protocols", with Triton extensions to the KServe protocol. Triton README: "based on the community developed KServe protocol".
- Triton model configuration, model warmup (https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/triton-inference-server/user-guide/docs/user_guide/model_configuration.html#model-warmup): model not shown as ready until configured warmup completes.
- gRPC deadlines guide (https://grpc.io/docs/guides/deadlines/): "By default, gRPC does not set a deadline", advice to always set a realistic one, `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED` on expiry, propagation supported by some implementations and explicitly enabled in some languages.
- Triton batcher docs (https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/triton-inference-server/user-guide/docs/user_guide/batcher.html): queue-policy field names (see lesson 02).

Not claimed or checked: default ports (the YAML says its path and port are examples), trace header formats, Prometheus metric names, shadow-traffic tooling, and retry-policy settings in specific clients. The probe YAML and numbers are placeholders and were not run (no cluster).
